solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: We lost with Boris – one should go and just look around

indicators.note: one should go tells you to drop the letter I, the numeral for one, from what precedes
something lost has wandered off its proper course, so these letters stray out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written
the name with its I removed

explanation.surface: A rueful political lament: the party lost under Boris Johnson, so he should quit and just wander about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One should go' reads like a call for a resignation, but it removes the I from the name before the remaining letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To browse is to look over things casually, as in a shop, without any firm intention of buying.

clue.text: Boris source, describing downfall – "brilliant!"

indicators.note: a source is where a river starts, so only the opening letter of the name is taken

blocks.note: the initial of the name
a downfall can be a shower of rain, and the adjective describing such weather

explanation.surface: An insider describing Boris Johnson's fall from power with one gleeful exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' suggests political ruin, but here it is literal precipitation, and 'describing' asks for the word that describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone brilliant is highly intelligent and clever, which is exactly what calling a person brainy means.

clue.text: Provincial place finding Iran too 'other'?

indicators.note: making something other means changing it into a different form, so these letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A puzzled geography question about some small-town place that regards Iran as foreign too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provincial' sounds like a sneer at small-town attitudes, but it is literal: the answer is one of Canada's provinces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is a province of Canada, so it is quite literally a place of provincial status within that country.

clue.text: Could it really make Trump any less intelligible on the phone?

definitions.text: Could it really make Trump any less intelligible on the phone?

blocks.clueFragment: Could it really make Trump any less intelligible
blocks.note: the surface reading: a jibe that the US president's speech is already garbled enough
the setter's reading: a telephone device that encodes speech so eavesdroppers cannot understand it

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is political: Trump's rambling talk is supposedly so confused that a device for encrypting calls could hardly make it harder to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A telephone scrambler distorts the voice signal so that anyone listening in without the decoder hears only gibberish.

clue.text: Brenda's more swanky upmarket transport?

indicators.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, so the words are as pronounced in her cut-glass accent

blocks.note: more swanky is more posh, which a plummy royal voice draws out into two syllables

explanation.surface: A satirical guess at which smart vehicle the Queen would deem classier than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls Queen Elizabeth II Brenda; in a very upper-class accent the comparative of posh comes out like the German sports-car maker's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Porsche is an expensive German sports car, a luxury way of getting around.

clue.text: see 9dn.
Party independent leader has no back passage

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so just the opening letter of the preceding word is kept
going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: a sect is a faction or party within a larger body
its first letter
taken as written before it is turned round

explanation.surface: A crude jibe that the head of an independent party has no rear passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back passage' looks like innuendo, but 'back' turns round the word before it and 'passage' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage of a book or piece of music is a portion of it, which is also called a section.

clue.text: Zero weight gained after short vacation? A deceptive image

blocks.note: hol is the British clipped form of holiday, the usual word for a vacation
the figure nought looks like the letter
a gram is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A dieter returns from a brief trip having put on no weight, but suspects the scales are lying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gained after' tells you the zero and the weight come after the short break, rather than describing weight gain.
explanation.definitionFit: A hologram is a three-dimensional picture made with lasers that seems solid but is only an optical illusion.

clue.text: Waste time with a daft run or jogging

indicators.note: to jog is to jolt or shake, and shaken things end up in a different order

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on recreational running as a pointless way to fill an afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jogging' fits the running picture so neatly that it is easy to miss it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To fart around is vulgar slang for messing about idly and achieving nothing, frittering hours away.

clue.text: ( &27ac./5dn.) Crazy expenditure, Andrew! Hallo – might this reveal how you got the money?

definitions.text: might this reveal how you got the money?

indicators.note: something crazy is deranged, its parts thrown out of their sensible order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone greets Prince Andrew and asks pointedly how his lavish spending is funded.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder spans the whole first sentence; the familiar name and greeting are there just for their letters. The surface jabs at Prince Andrew's opaque finances.
explanation.definitionFit: In UK law this court order compels a person to explain the legitimate source of assets that seem beyond their known income.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) Possible cure for randy types: getting around ancient spa town

blocks.note: c is short for circa, Latin for around
a plain synonym
Bath in Somerset is famous for its Roman spa

explanation.surface: Advice that lustful folk should take a trip round a historic spa town to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container signal, but it simply gives c, the abbreviation for circa used with approximate dates.
explanation.definitionFit: A plunge into icy water is the traditional remedy prescribed for dampening sexual ardour, hence a possible cure.

clue.text: County TV presenter on edge

blocks.note: Ant McPartlin, of the British TV double act Ant and Dec
a plain synonym

explanation.surface: A TV host from somewhere in the provinces is said to be anxious and on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' reads as nervous, but 'on' just places one piece next to the other and 'edge' is a synonym. Ant and Dec are a hugely popular British presenting duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, in the north-east of the province.

clue.text: Only half of arse covered by naff singer's ornaments

indicators.note: keeping only half of a word means the remaining letters are dropped
naff is British slang for shoddy or rubbish, so the word is botched into a new arrangement
what is covered by something sits inside it, enclosed on both sides

blocks.note: the front two of its four letters
the word without its possessive

explanation.surface: A cheesy pop star's bottom is said to be half concealed by tacky decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged six letters are split after the first E to take the two letters inside. Arse is British slang for backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Earrings are pieces of jewellery worn on the ear lobes, a common kind of personal decoration.

clue.text: Figure at work, making a stinking pile?

blocks.note: a doll is a small figure of a person
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone at the office is accused of producing a malodorous heap, perhaps of bad work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure at work' sounds like a person in the office; 'at' only places the second piece beside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollop is a shapeless lump of something soft, and the question mark flags a smelly pile as only one example.

clue.text: Gangster's $1000 to perform a castration?

blocks.note: a G or grand is slang for a thousand dollars
to unman is to deprive of manhood, literally to castrate

explanation.surface: A mobster's fee for a particularly brutal punishment job.
explanation.walkthrough: The dollar sum looks like a hitman's price, which suits the picture, but it is simply the single letter used in slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A gangster is a criminal who often carries and uses a firearm, so is an armed man or gunman.

clue.text: Talent associated with hack (maybe you should avoid oral examination)

definitions.text: maybe you should avoid oral examination

blocks.note: a gift is a natural talent
a hack is a horse for ordinary riding

explanation.surface: Commentary on a journalist's knack, with a sly aside about avoiding a viva or a dentist's check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' wants to be a writer, but it is a riding horse. The definition alludes to the proverb: don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb warns against inspecting a present's teeth to judge its age, so checking its mouth is exactly what you should not do.

clue.text: Tabloid hell: back to front cover-up

indicators.note: back to front here means the rear letter is moved round to the very start

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
Hades is the underworld of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A furious headline about a newspaper's hellish attempt to conceal a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover-up' suggests a scandal being hushed, but a sunshade literally covers you from the sun. Only the final letter of the underworld moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunshade such as a parasol or awning provides cover overhead, keeping off strong sunlight.

clue.text: Drone's mechanism finally complete

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: its last letter
utter means total or complete, as in utter nonsense

explanation.surface: A report that an unmanned aircraft's machinery is at last finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drone' suggests an unmanned aircraft, but it is the low monotonous sound of someone talking.
explanation.definitionFit: A drone is a low continuous murmuring sound, and a mutter is likewise an indistinct, low-voiced grumble.

clue.text: Drunk's hotel room state?

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for very intoxicated
second meaning: wrecked, as rock stars notoriously leave their rooms

explanation.surface: Asking what condition the hotel room was left in by a drunken guest.
explanation.walkthrough: One adjective covers both the inebriated guest and the smashed-up room they leave behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang word means both thoroughly intoxicated and comprehensively wrecked or vandalised by a reveller.

clue.text: Sources of "frank exchange", in fact, laughably fake

indicators.note: sources are where things begin, so only the first letter of each word is taken
something done laughably is ridiculous and absurd, so the letters are muddled into a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of each word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sceptical note that a supposedly candid exchange of views is actually a risible sham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fake' at the end looks like part of the description of the exchange; it is a verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To affect an emotion or manner is to put it on or pretend to have it, which is to feign it.

clue.text: Drink, I say, before getting laid ineptly

indicators.note: done ineptly means done clumsily and badly, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like I say
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a stiff drink before a clumsy sexual encounter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting laid' reads as one phrase; 'before getting' is the positional link and 'laid' alone is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial is a sweet fruit-flavoured drink, often diluted, or in older use a liqueur.

clue.text: Grand being in fast hospital for the duration

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is housed within another

blocks.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand
Lent is the Christian season of fasting
the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A grand patient stays in hospital, starving, for as long as it takes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like an adjective for speed, but it is the noun for a period of abstinence.
explanation.definitionFit: Length can mean the extent of time something lasts, so it is a synonym for duration.

clue.text: Pair of tits: one with name 'Killer'

blocks.note: a tit is a fool, as is an ass, and a pair gives two of them
the Roman numeral
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Saucy innuendo about a bosom, with a gangster-film nickname tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tits' plays on its bawdy sense, but in British slang a tit is an idiot, just like an ass.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a person who murders someone, typically a prominent figure, for political motives or money.

clue.text: Was a PR person about right to deliver a contemptuous rejection?

indicators.note: about here means round or surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: public relations people put a spin on stories, so in the past tense they spun
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a publicist was correct to brush off a request with scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was a PR person' is a whole phrase meaning did what spin doctors do; 'about' then puts it round the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn someone or something is to reject it with disdain, turning it away scornfully.

clue.text: Stinger has Randy getting end away – "earth trembled, initially"

indicators.note: getting the end away means the final letter is sent off and dropped
initially means at the start, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: randy means horny, which then loses its final letter
the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: A tabloid confession: Randy had sex and the earth moved, as the cliché goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting your end away' is British slang for having sex, which makes the deletion signal read as pure smut. Randy is British for lustful, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A hornet is a large wasp with a painful sting, so it is literally an insect that stings.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Beleaguered EU resigned to reform

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A beset European Union reluctantly accepts it must change its ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resigned to reform' reads as an idiom of grudging acceptance; 'to reform' is the signal and the two words before it are the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Beleaguered originally meant surrounded by an army, and figuratively means harassed by troubles, exactly the state of being besieged.

clue.text: Gin drunk after sex direction?

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about all over the place, so the letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: head is slang for oral sex
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunken night ends with a question about which way the evening is going after sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the rearranged spirit behind the slang word, so the clue reads backwards from its surface order.
explanation.definitionFit: A heading is a compass bearing, the course in which a ship or aircraft is travelling.
